procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 8th February, 1985 of the High Court of Delhi quashing the complaint and summoning order.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused persons filed petitions under s. 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code in the High Court for quashing the complaint, which were allowed. Delhi High Court by its judgment dated 8th February, 1985 quashed the complaint.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Deputy Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, filed a Special Leave Petition in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court granted special leave, allowed the appeal, and set aside the High Court's order, thereby reinstating the complaint.

directions: The order and judgment quashing the proceedings are set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can quash a complaint based on facts subsequently discovered that pertain to the truth or falsity of the allegations.

facts: The High Court, exercising its power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, quashed a criminal complaint.
The High Court's decision was based on two main grounds: a subsequent report by the CBI and the fact that some alleged co-conspirators were not named as parties in the complaint.
These grounds relate to facts discovered after the complaint was filed and pertain to the potential truth or falsity of the original allegations.
law: The power of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC to quash a complaint is limited and well-settled.
The correct test is to take all the allegations in the complaint as true, without adding or subtracting anything, and determine if a prima facie case is made out.
Facts subsequently discovered to prove the truth or falsity of the allegations in a complaint are not a valid ground for quashing the complaint at this stage.
The question at the stage of a quashing petition is not whether the allegations are true, but whether they constitute a cognizable offense.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by considering the subsequent CBI report and the non-inclusion of other parties.
The Court reasoned that these are not valid grounds for quashing a complaint where a Magistrate has already taken cognizance based on a prima facie case.
The truthfulness of the allegations, including the evidence from the CBI report, is a matter to be investigated and determined during the trial, not in a Section 482 proceeding.
By delving into the truth of the matter, the High Court improperly used its extraordinary power.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's approach, holding that a complaint cannot be quashed under Section 482 based on subsequently discovered facts that go to the truth or falsity of the allegations. The Court ruled that the High Court's role is limited to determining if the complaint, taken at face value, makes out a prima facie case. The actual truth of the allegations is a matter for trial. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether a criminal proceeding can be quashed on the ground that some of the parties alleged to be involved in the conspiracy were not made parties to the case.

facts: The High Court had quashed a criminal complaint.
One of the reasons for quashing the complaint was that some of the parties alleged to be involved in the conspiracy, such as the Bank, were not made parties to the case.
law: Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives a court ample power to add any person as an accused during the trial if evidence against them emerges.

The power of a High Court to quash proceedings under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is limited and should be used very sparingly, only when no prima facie case is made out from the allegations in the complaint.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that the fact that some alleged conspirators were not made parties is "no ground for quashing the criminal proceedings."

The Court reasoned that the issue of non-included parties is not a fatal flaw because the trial court can use its powers under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to add them as accused later if sufficient evidence is presented.
By quashing the complaint on this basis, the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected this argument, holding that a criminal proceeding cannot be quashed merely because some individuals alleged to be part of a conspiracy were not initially named as parties in the case. The Court clarified that such individuals can be added as accused later in the trial if necessary.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by quashing the proceedings when, taking the allegations in the complaint as true, a prima facie case was made out.

facts: The High Court, exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), quashed a criminal complaint.

The High Court's decision was based on two main grounds: 1) a subsequent report by the CBI that had not yet been proven, and 2) the fact that some individuals alleged to be part of the conspiracy were not named as parties in the complaint.
law: The jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash a complaint is limited.
The established test is that the court must take all allegations in the complaint as true, without adding or subtracting anything.
Proceedings can only be quashed if, based on the face of the complaint, no prima facie case for trial is made out.
The truth or falsity of the allegations is a matter to be investigated during the trial, not at the stage of a Section 482 petition.
application: The Supreme Court held that the grounds used by the High Court were not valid for quashing the proceedings, especially after a Magistrate had already taken cognizance of the complaint based on a prima facie case.
The Court reasoned that considering an unproven CBI report and the non-inclusion of other parties went beyond the permissible scope of a Section 482 inquiry.
By doing so, the High Court improperly delved into the merits and truth of the allegations, which is the function of the trial court.

The Supreme Court found that taking the allegations in the complaint as true, a prima facie case was established, and therefore, the High Court should not have used its extraordinary power to quash it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC. The Court held that the High Court's reasons for quashing the complaint were invalid at that stage. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can quash a complaint based on facts subsequently discovered that pertain to the truth or falsity of the allegations.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's jurisdiction under Section 482 is limited to determining if a prima facie case is made out from the allegations in the complaint itself. It should not delve into the truth or falsity of the allegations by conducting a mini-trial or considering external materials like a government concession or a circular (I.P.O. Circular No. 14/82) that were not part of the initial complaint.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in considering subsequent facts, such as the government's concession that a paragraph in the complaint could not be relied upon, to determine that the complaint was baseless. This is a proper exercise of its inherent power under Section 482 to prevent an abuse of the process of the court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a criminal proceeding can be quashed on the ground that some of the parties alleged to be involved in the conspiracy were not made parties to the case.
appellant_arguments: The non-inclusion of some alleged co-conspirators is not a valid legal ground for quashing a criminal proceeding against the accused who have been named and against whom a prima facie case of conspiracy is made out in the complaint.
respondent_arguments: The failure to implead all necessary parties involved in the alleged conspiracy makes the complaint defective and demonstrates the weakness or arbitrariness of the prosecution's case, thereby justifying the quashing of the proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by quashing the proceedings when, taking the allegations in the complaint as true, a prima facie case was made out.
appellant_arguments: The complaint, when taken at face value, clearly alleged a conspiracy and the commission of substantive offences under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act. As these allegations made out a prima facie case, the High Court exceeded its limited jurisdiction by substituting its own judgment on the merits (e.g., that 'there was no conspiracy') for that of the trial court.
respondent_arguments: The High Court acted within its jurisdiction because the complaint was baseless and did not disclose a sufficient case to proceed. The judge correctly concluded that 'no legalistic view should be taken' and quashed the complaint to prevent an abuse of the court's process, as there was 'no case to proceed'.

statutes.act_name: The Act (unspecified, under which the Import Control Order, 1955 was passed)

cases.case_name: Bennett Coleman & Co. & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
cases.principle: The power of the Control Order could only be exercised by Government notification and not by notice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The extraordinary inherent power of the court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should not be used to quash a complaint at a preliminary stage, as the truth or otherwise of the allegations is a matter to be investigated at the time of trial.
obiter: The principles on which a complaint can be quashed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are well-settled.
The court is not expressing any opinion on the merit of the charge, and the accused persons would be entitled to prove before the court that no charge has been made out against them.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by quashing the complaint. The court's role at this stage is not to determine the truth of the allegations, but only to assess whether, taking the complaint's allegations as true, a prima facie case has been made out. By delving into the merits, considering a subsequent CBI report, and finding no conspiracy, the High Court improperly conducted a mini-trial and usurped the function of the trial court.
legal_tests_applied: The limit of the power to be exercised by the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to determine if a prima facie case for trial has been made out by 'Taking all the allegations in the complaint to be true, without adding. or subtracting anything'.

reasoning_for_decision.reason: The High Court improperly based its decision on subsequent facts and the merits of the case, which is beyond the scope of a Section 482 inquiry.
supporting_quotes: We are not concerned with the truth or otherwise of the allegations made in the complaint, that would be investigated at the time of the trial.

reasoning_for_decision.reason: The grounds relied upon by the High Court, namely a subsequent CBI report and the non-inclusion of all alleged co-conspirators, are not valid legal grounds for quashing a criminal proceeding where cognizance has already been taken.
supporting_quotes: The grounds upon which the learned judge seems to have quashed the complaint in the instant case was the subsequent report by the CBI which had not yet been proved and considered in the background of the allegations made and secondly that some of the parties alleged to be in the conspiracy were not made parties. These, in our opinion, are no grounds for quashing the criminal proceedings where on prima facie being satisfied the learned Metropolitan Magistrate had taken cognizance.

reasoning_for_decision.reason: When the allegations in the complaint are taken as true, a prima facie case was established, and therefore the High Court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings.
supporting_quotes: Taking all the allegations in the complaint to be true, without adding. or subtracting anything, at this stag.,._ it cannot be said that no prima facie case for trial had been+. made out. That is the limit of the power to be exercised by the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court in the instant cae" has exceeded that jurisdiction.

policy_considerations: The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an 'extraordinary power' that should not be used to stifle a legitimate prosecution when a prima facie case is apparent from the complaint.
